Red flag present (painful vesicles, widespread erosions, rapidly enlarging ulcer)?
Escalate: prompt antiviral therapy for herpes superinfection; treat sepsis
Skin biopsy for acantholysis; ATP2A2 gene testing; swabs if infected
Does biopsy or ATP2A2 testing confirm Darier disease?
Consider Hailey-Hailey disease, Grover disease or pemphigus
Advise trigger avoidance: heat, sweat, sun and friction
Topical retinoids, corticosteroids and keratolytics for mild to moderate disease
Acitretin for severe or widespread disease
Antibiotics for secondary infection; antivirals for herpes superinfection
Chronic relapsing; most maintain control with skin care and trigger avoidance

cells.text: Suprabasal acantholysis with dyskeratotic corps ronds and grains
Loss-of-function ATP2A2 variant, the cause of the disease

rows.parameter: Viral swab or PCR for herpes simplex

cells.text: Herpes superinfection when sudden painful worsening occurs
Bacterial infection of malodorous or eroded lesions
Nail and palmar signs that clinch the diagnosis
Flexural involvement is easily mistaken for it
Sudden painful monomorphic vesicles or erosions
Heat, sweating, sunlight and friction; cool loose clothing, sun protection and emollients

rows.parameter: Topical therapy for mild to moderate disease

cells.text: Topical retinoids, topical corticosteroids and keratolytics
Acitretin for severe or widespread disease
Antibiotics for secondary bacterial infection; prompt antiviral therapy for herpes
Antiseptics and topical antimicrobials for malodour and maceration
Screen for and support associated mood disorders
Autosomal dominant ATP2A2 disorder; surgery or laser for resistant localised disease

flowcharts.title: Diagnosis and management of Dejerine-Roussy thalamic pain syndrome

nodes.text: Suspected Dejerine-Roussy syndrome: delayed central pain after a thalamic stroke
Red flag present (evolving deficit, tumour features, intractable pain with depression)?
Urgent: assess for recurrent stroke or a structural lesion such as tumour
MRI for contralateral thalamic infarct; diffusion imaging; quantitative sensory testing
Does MRI show a thalamic infarct or haemorrhage on the opposite side?
Consider peripheral pain, brainstem or cortical stroke, or functional disorder
Amitriptyline, gabapentinoids or duloxetine first-line for central pain
Lamotrigine as an adjunct, with evidence in central post-stroke pain
Antiplatelet therapy and vascular risk-factor control to prevent further injury
Treat depression, anxiety and sleep disturbance that amplify the pain
Refer to a pain service; consider neuromodulation for refractory pain
Often chronic and hard to control; partial relief is common, full resolution uncommon

rows.parameter: Diffusion-weighted imaging in the acute phase

cells.text: Painful hemibody presentation; thalamic lesion on MRI separates it
Features suggesting tumour rather than infarct
Delayed post-stroke pain is wrongly called functional
Amitriptyline, gabapentinoids or duloxetine rather than conventional analgesics
Alternative or adjunct with evidence in central post-stroke pain
Antiplatelet therapy and vascular risk-factor modification
Depression, anxiety and sleep disturbance amplify central pain
Consider motor cortex or deep brain stimulation for refractory pain
Stroke medicine, pain medicine and psychology

flowcharts.title: Diagnosis and management of health care-associated infection

nodes.text: New fever or organ dysfunction in a hospital patient
Onset after 48 to 72 h of admission?
Manage as community-acquired infection
Examine devices and wounds; cultures before antibiotics
Bacteriuria only, without urinary symptoms?
Do not treat; remove catheter if not needed
Pneumonia with MDR risk or high local resistance?
Single agent without MDR risk
Antipseudomonal beta-lactam plus second agent plus MRSA cover
Source control: remove infected line or device
Contact precautions and notify infection prevention
De-escalate on cultures; 7 days for HAP or VAP

cells.text: Earlier onset counts as community-acquired or from the transferring site
IV antibiotics within 90 days, 5 or more hospital days, septic shock, ARDS, renal replacement
Prior IV antibiotics is the strongest predictor
Do not culture or treat, except in pregnancy
Most common US hospital infection; recent antibiotics main trigger
Spores survive alcohol gel; soap and water plus sporicide
Negative pressure with at least 12 air changes per hour
Onset within 48 to 72 h of admission
Bacteriuria with no urinary symptoms; confusion often unrelated

cells.text: Health care-associated pneumonia without MDR risk
Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h, or moxifloxacin 400 mg, ciprofloxacin 400 mg q8h or levofloxacin 750 mg IV q24h, or ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV q6h, or ertapenem 1 g IV q24h
Ceftazidime 2 g q8h, cefepime 2 g q8 to 12h, piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g q6h, imipenem 500 mg q6h or meropenem 1 g q8h

Linezolid 600 mg IV q12h or vancomycin 15 mg/kg q12h
Unit MRSA above 10 to 20% of S. aureus, unknown prevalence, or risk factor
De-escalate; stop using procalcitonin plus clinical criteria
Colonised or infected MDR, C. auris, C. difficile
